title: Whoa! A Faraway Planet Might Have Air Like Earth!
summary:
Imagine a world where the sky isn’t just empty space—it’s filled with air, maybe even clouds! For the first time ever, scientists have spotted an atmosphere around a rocky planet that’s in the “habitable zone” of its star. That’s the not-too-hot, not-too-cold region where liquid water could exist. And water means a chance for life!

The planet is called LHS 1140 b. It’s about 48 light-years away—that’s so far, if you could fly at the speed of light, it’d take 48 years to get there! It’s a super-Earth, meaning it’s bigger than our planet but not a giant gas ball like Jupiter. It’s about 5.6 times heavier than Earth. Brrr, it’s cold there: minus 53 degrees Fahrenheit on the surface. But with an atmosphere, it might be warmer, like wearing a cozy blanket.

So, how did they find this invisible air? They didn’t see the atmosphere directly. Instead, they used a giant telescope in Chile to watch the planet pass in front of its star. As starlight shone through the planet’s edge, they looked for a tiny dip in a special kind of light—infrared light—that helium gas blocks. It’s like seeing a shadow that tells you something is there. And they found it! Helium was leaking from the planet into space.

What’s extra cool? A smaller, hotter planet next door, LHS 1140 c, showed no helium at all. That means its atmosphere probably got blasted away long ago by the star’s radiation. But LHS 1140 b, sitting farther out, held onto its air for billions of years. That’s a big deal because the star is a red dwarf, which can be really mean and strip atmospheres away. This planet is a survivor!

Does this mean there are aliens? No—at least not yet. The helium only tells us the upper atmosphere is there. We still don’t know if it has oxygen or water vapor. But scientists are super excited. “It’s absolutely exciting!” said one expert. Next, they’ll try to figure out what the rest of the air is made of. Maybe one day, we’ll find a planet that’s just like home.
why_it_matters: Discovering an atmosphere on a faraway planet could one day lead to finding another world like Earth, which might change how you think about our place in the universe.

background_read: Scientists have found thousands of planets outside our solar system, but very few of them are rocky and in the habitable zone where water could exist as liquid.
Red dwarf stars are the most common type of star in the universe, and many of them have planets orbiting them.
Finding helium in a planet's atmosphere is exciting because it hints that the planet might have held onto its air for billions of years, despite harsh radiation from its star.
Article_Structure: WHO: Scientists watching the planet LHS 1140 b using a telescope.
WHAT: Detected a helium atmosphere around a rocky super-Earth in the habitable zone.
WHERE: In space, 48 light-years away; observed from a telescope in Chile.
WHY: To find planets that might have conditions for life, and to understand how atmospheres survive around red dwarf stars.

perspectives.description: Scientists are thrilled because this is the first time an atmosphere has been found on a rocky planet in the habitable zone, which makes the search for life more promising.
Some people remind us that finding helium is just a small clue; we still don't know if the planet has oxygen or water, which are needed for life as we know it.
Researchers now want to look more closely at the planet's air to see what other gases are there, which could take years of study.
